text: Once a deploy updates the GitOps repo, the real question becomes: how does the new version actually reach live traffic? All at once, or gradually? Canary and blue-green are the two real answers, and they make very different tradeoffs.

Canary doesn't replace the old version all at once. It routes a small percentage of real traffic — commonly 10% — to the new version, while the rest keeps hitting the version that's already proven stable. If it looks healthy, the weight steps up: 10, then 25, then 50, then 100, pausing at each step to watch. The name comes from sending a canary ahead into a coal mine — if something's wrong, you find out at a small cost before everyone's exposed to it. Traffic splitting at this level is usually handled by a service mesh or ingress controller, not the application itself.

Blue-green works completely differently. You run two full, independent environments. Blue is the current live version, serving 100% of traffic, untouched. Green gets the new version deployed and tested in full before any real user ever reaches it. Once green checks out, you switch all traffic in one move — repointing a load balancer or swapping a Kubernetes Service's selector — and blue stays running, idle, as an instant rollback target if anything's wrong.

Here's what that canary weight actually looks like as a real Argo Rollouts strategy. setWeight sends that percentage of traffic to the new ReplicaSet, and pause holds it there for the given duration before the controller even considers advancing to the next step. Nothing here decides on its own whether it's safe to move forward — that's still a human, or the automation you'll see next lesson.

So which one do you pick? Canary's advantage is blast radius — a bug only ever touches a small slice of users before the rollout can be halted — but it needs real traffic-splitting infrastructure, and some bugs only appear once the percentage climbs. Blue-green's advantage is rollback speed and environment parity — green is fully tested before it ever sees traffic, and rolling back is one switch, not a walk-back. Its cost is that the cutover is all-or-nothing, and it usually means paying for two full environments during the overlap.

Most teams don't pick one pattern for everything — blue-green for a low-traffic internal service, canary for a customer-facing checkout flow. Either way, every pause in that canary rollout only helps if something is actually watching the metrics. That's progressive delivery, and it's next.
